faq.q: How do I know if I'm really hungry?
faq.a: Physical hunger builds gradually and shows up in your body: a rumbling stomach, low energy or trouble concentrating, usually a few hours after your last meal. It's open to many foods and can wait a little. If you ate recently, your stomach is quiet and you want one specific food right now, the urge is more likely emotional.

No. Eating for comfort or celebration now and then is a normal part of life. It becomes worth looking at when food is your main way of coping with feelings, or when it leaves you feeling guilty or out of control.

faq.q: Why do I crave sweets when I'm stressed or tired?
faq.a: Sweet, salty and crunchy foods change how you feel quickly and reliably, so it's easy to learn to reach for them when you're stressed, bored or tired. That's a habit, not a character flaw. Noticing the pattern, for example with a short check-in before you eat, is the first step to choosing on purpose.

HALT stands for hungry, angry, lonely, tired. It's a long-standing slogan from addiction-recovery communities, and it works well as a quick check before you eat: if you're angry, lonely or tired rather than hungry, food may not be what you need most.

faq.q: What's the difference between emotional eating and binge eating?
faq.a: Emotional eating is common and broad: eating in response to feelings rather than hunger. Binge eating disorder is a clinical condition with recurring episodes of eating a large amount while feeling a loss of control, often followed by distress. If that sounds familiar, please talk to a doctor or an eating-disorder service.

faq.q: Can an app help with emotional eating?
faq.a: An app can help you notice. Recording how hungry you are and how you feel when you eat is one of the most common recommendations for understanding emotional eating, and Fimbl's meal check-ins are built for exactly that. An app isn't a treatment, though, and it's no substitute for professional help when eating feels out of control.
